title: Economic cache decider and safety runner for KV/prefix TTL tuning
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description:
Goal: Build a decision engine that recommends per-prefix TTL adjustments plus a lightweight 'safety runner' that validates recommendations via shadow replays and staged application. The tool should produce a ranked set of config diffs (TTL, key normalization rules, retention buckets) with estimated cost delta, latency impact, and uncertainty estimates. It must be safe to run in production: a staged validation flow (shadow -> partial apply -> gradual rollout) with automated abort/rollback criteria.

Approach:
- Hit-rate modeling: develop a probabilistic model that predicts prefix hit probability as a function of prefix age, recent request frequency, and observed affiliation to affinity cohorts. Use heteroscedastic logistic regression with L1 regularization for interpretability and a Bayesian bootstrap to report confidence intervals. Model outputs: expected hit-rate lift for an increase/decrease in TTL, variance estimate, and a sensitivity score per prefix.
- Economic simulation: replay sampled traces (stratified by prefix popularity deciles and tenant class) through an offline simulator that models batching effects, KV cache eviction dynamics, and per-token GPU cost. Produce a cost-benefit curve for each candidate TTL change (expected cost savings vs expected increase in model invocation rate).
- Safety runner: a small, orchestrated harness to run shadow traffic for 1-24 hours, collect metrics (token cost, request latency P50/P95/P99, error rate, cache lookup QPS, hit-rate delta), and compute an aggregate safety score. The runner implements abort rules: immediate abort for P99 latency increase > 10% relative or backend error rate increase > 0.1% absolute; soft abort if cost savings are below threshold given model uncertainty.
- Config apply strategy: produce JSON diffs consumable by the config service with metadata: confidence, rollback window, sampling percentage, and expected cost delta. Integrate with the Console rollout APIs for gradual percentage ramp and automatic rollback.

Trade-offs & open questions:
- Conservative TTLs reduce risk but miss cost savings; we need tunable risk appetite per customer tier.
- Strong correlation between batch size and hit-rate: longer TTLs increase probability of cache hits but may reduce effective batching opportunities for some workloads — simulator must model this.
- Cold-start prefixes (new tenants/flows) require default heuristics to avoid brittle TTL shrinkage.

Success metrics:
- Safety: zero SEV incidents attributable to this feature in first 90 days of rollout.
- Economics: 10-25% per-prefix KV cost reduction for cohorts where recommendations were applied.
- Precision: >75% of applied TTL changes should match offline simulation direction (i.e., measured cost delta within predicted 20% band).
updates: 2026-02-22: Prototype hit-rate model (heteroscedastic logistic regression) trained on 7 days of production traces; baseline R2-like metrics indicate good explanatory power on popularity features.

2026-02-27: Built stratified trace-sampler and offline simulator. Early sim shows a 18% median token-cost reduction on medium-traffic tenants when applying per-prefix TTL increases with conservative confidence thresholds.

2026-03-02: Identified interaction: increasing TTL for hot prefixes sometimes increases mean batch latency slightly due to earlier token emission; added batch model to simulator to predict latency delta under SLOs.
2026-03-05: Design review with Runtime and Console teams. Feedback: expose confidence and rollback-window in config diffs; Console needs an endpoint for 'safety runner' telemetry ingestion.

2026-03-08: Implemented safety-runner prototype that runs 1% shadow traffic and emits metrics to /console/api/safety/kv-tuning. Initial shadow run on internal dev cluster completed, no latency regressions observed in 3-hour window.

2026-03-10: PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8123 — includes simulator integration and a minimal API for config diffs. Tagging for cross-team review. Next: add automated abort criteria and tie into Console rollouts.

Next steps: extend model to multi-tenant priors, add Bayesian bootstrap scoring to rank recommendations, instrument rollback automation in Console, and schedule a limited customer pilot (Select Dedicated customers).
